item.title: Major US outlets boycott shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cje3rezd92y3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Major US outlets boycott shared Trump coverage in protest at media ban - Published Major US television networks suspended their pooled coverage of President Donald Trump on Monday in response to CNN, Politico and MS NOW being barred from the White House. Trump announced the ban on Friday as he accused the organisations of writing "fiction or lies" about his administration. The companies said their reporters were denied access to the building on Saturday. The three US outlets have since said they will sue the Trump administration in a bid to "defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports". Shortly after, the White House launched its own streaming channel, Trump TV, which operates a 24/7 feed of clips of the president. Several other US outlets have also announced that they would not participate in coverage of pooled events, with some, including the New York Times and Washington Post, saying they would not share still images from Trump events on Monday. It meant there was no network TV footage of Trump boarding Air Force One or arriving in New York to attend the UN general assembly. Trump also took part in a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the new Marine One helipad on the White House South Lawn. The event was streamed on the White House site but his comments were inaudible. The president did later appear on television following a meeting with the Mayor of New York Zohran Mamdani. He told the president that all members of the media would be welcome at the press conference. Trump said: "It's interesting because, they said they were going to boycott me, but they never boycott me, so I wasn't very worried about that. Look at all that press." The pool involves media organisations sharing material to save on costs and space when broadcasting presidential events to the American public. Fox News Washington bureau chief Bryan Boughton, who currently holds a rotating role helping to organise media TV crews covering the White House, wrote in an email seen by the BBC that "effective today, the TV pool will not be covering designated as pool coverage" of Trump. The message said the move followed the White House "preventing" CNN from fulfilling its pool duties for Trump's trip to New York and that "there will be no replacement pool put in place". The three media organisations banned from the White House filed a lawsuit on Monday in US District Court in Washington. A joint statement announcing the legal action said: "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. "Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference." Related topics - Published10 hours ago - Published2 days ago

item.title: Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5yw8npxzrlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Lithuania ready to 'fight back' but has evacuation plans in face of Russia threats, PM tells BBC - Published Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace. He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams. Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. "We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly," Sinkevičius told the BBC. "We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us." Sinkevičius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". Last week Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Lithuania has experienced numerous incidents in the past year, which it describes as "hybrid attacks" and blames on neighbouring Belarus, a close Russian ally. Late on Monday night, flights were disrupted at Lithuania's main airport in the capital Vilnius, because of what the airports operator called a "hybrid attack carried out by Belarus", involving objects that appeared to resemble the shape of balloons. The president's chief adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said on Tuesday it was unclear whether the objects were balloons. Germany - a fellow Nato ally - pledged to permanently station a combat-ready brigade in Lithuania in 2023 as a response to the changing security situation in Europe. It is expected to be operational by 2027 and to number about 5,000 soldiers and civilian employees, though it has failed to recruit enough personnel voluntarily and is now turning to compulsory assignments to fill some positions. The majority of troops will be based in Rūdninkai, near the Suwałki Gap - a line that borders Lithuania and Poland and also links Belarus with Russia's Kaliningrad. Nato said that as of December last year it had more than 5,000 troops stationed in Lithuania. The origins of last week's drone incident over Lithuania have not been confirmed, however Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it had come from the direction of Belarus. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace. "We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory." Moscow did not comment on the incident. Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine. Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel. Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year. Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones. Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one Nato member shall be considered an attack against all members". item.title: Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwm2qpmepmlzo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Iran must stop arming Houthis in Yemen, G7 says ahead of UN General Assembly - Published Iran must "end its arming of and support" for the Houthis in Yemen, the foreign ministers of G7 nations have said in a joint statement. The G7 also condemned "in the strongest terms" Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, adding that the recent escalation in fighting against Saudi-backed pro-government forces in Yemen represented a threat to regional and global energy security. Thousands of refugees have fled Yemen in recent days after the Iran-backed group seized territory along the country's Red Sea coastline, including near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the gateway to a key global shipping route. Iran has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically. The G7 statement comes ahead of the annual UN General Assembly in New York, where Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian is due to speak. "We call on the Houthis to immediately cease all military actions, all threats and attacks against civilian shipping, and to return to the political process in good faith," said the foreign ministers of the UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States. It went on: "Their reprehensible actions constitute a dangerous pattern of escalation that risks further exacerbating the conflict, undermining international trade and creating global economic instability." "Looking forward, we will continue to support the legitimate Government of Yemen and reaffirm our strong commitment to the unity, sovereignty, independence, and territorial integrity of Yemen," the ministers said. Their statement was issued following a meeting on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. - Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war - Published20 hours ago - Houthis say they targeted Saudi capital with ballistic missiles - Published2 days ago Meanwhile, at least six people were killed in Saudi strikes on the strategic Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mokha, the AFP news agency reported, citing Houthi-affiliated media. Two children and a woman were among the dead, while eight others were injured in the attack on the city, which the Houthis seized from pro-government forces earlier this month. Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen's government, has not yet commented on the reported strikes. The UN estimates that in all, more than 120,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the sudden surge in fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Earlier this month, the Houthis, who had already seized most of the populated parts of Yemen, took control of Bab al-Mandab, a narrow, maritime chokepoint where the southern Red Sea flows into the Gulf of Aden and the wider Indian Ocean. Saudi Arabia has retaliated with hundreds of air strikes in the region. The Houthis have also launched hundreds of drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia, including the capital city, Riyadh. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the UK will provide "defensive air-to-air refuelling" support for Saudi Arabia, involving a single British aircraft, a Voyager, based out of RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus. Burnham said the announcement followed a request from Saudi Arabia for "military support", which he agreed to on the advice of Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband. A diplomatic source told AFP that France has pledged support as well, and says is ready to work on "securing" Saudi energy infrastructure via a "strictly defensive approach". Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has also requested military support from President Donald Trump, US media reported. Trump has wavered for weeks over whether to act on a Saudi request for help in fighting the Houthis, the New York Times reported on Monday. The US president had earlier told Fox News that he was in "deciding mode" as he considered options for the next steps in the war against Iran. On Sunday, US embassies across the Middle East issued new security alerts as fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed coalition in Yemen intensified. The Houthis declare themselves to be part of the Iranian-led "axis of resistance" against Israel, the US and the wider West - along with armed group such as Hamas and Lebanon's Hezbollah movement. Although Iran has denied arming the Houthis in violation of a UN embargo, the UK and other Western powers have said their naval forces have repeatedly intercepted Iranian weapons shipments bound for Yemen during the civil war. A panel of UN experts also concluded in 2024 that the Houthis had been transformed into a powerful military organisation due to the transfer of materiel, assistance and training from Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Hezbollah and Iraqi specialists. Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated in 2015, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule. A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea. The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom. Since taking control of Bab al-Mandab, they have said they pose no threat to international shipping but reiterated that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

item.title: Eleven injured in shooting outside Turkish school
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6y0z4gv0le4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Eleven injured in shooting outside Turkish school - Published Eleven people have been injured in a shooting outside a high school in Turkey, with police detaining a 15-year-old male suspect. Two people were left in critical conditions after a gunman opened fire before fleeing on Tuesday morning, It happened at the Inci Uzmez Vocational and Technical Anatolian High School in the western province of Manisa, with the injured reportedly all students. The suspect's mother, father, and grandfather - who reportedly owned the weapon - have also been detained, according to the country's justice minister Akın Gürlek. It is the third school shooting in Turkey this year and comes as the government continues to grapple with how to address the recent spate of violence. CCTV footage appeared to show the suspect walking through empty streets checking a shotgun, which is clearly visible. He is casually dressed and appears unhurried. Later footage showed the apparent suspect, who is reportedly a student at the school, running from the scene with the weapon still in hand. The motive behind the attack was not immediately clear. According to Turkish law, the teenager is required to appear before a court before being officially arrested. In a statement, Turkey's education ministry said the incident had "deeply saddened our nation, and our educational community in particular". It said that three national investigators from the ministry had been sent to Manisa. Two deadly school shootings in April caused outrage in Turkey and led to new security measures for the 2026-2027 academic year, including tighter gun controls. Before then, the country did not have a history of school shootings. In an attack in Kahramanmaras, a 14-year-old killed nine students aged 10 and 11, and one teacher. The gunman died at the scene. - Published16 April

item.title: Sri Lankan court to deliver verdict on deadly Easter bombings
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw8r687nedzgo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Sri Lankan court to deliver verdict on deadly Easter bombings - Published A Sri Lankan court is set to rule on 24 people accused of plotting the 2019 Easter Sunday bomb attacks that killed 270 people and injured more than 500. The case against Naufer Moulavi, named as the main mastermind of the attacks, and 23 others has dragged on for years. The co-ordinated suicide attacks on multiple locations including several churches holding Easter mass and three luxury hotels were the deadliest Sri Lanka had seen since the end of its civil war in 2009. The associates and relatives of nine suicide bombers are among those facing more than 23,000 charges, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism and possessing firearms. All defendants have denied involvement. Investigators blame the attack on a homegrown Islamist extremist group. The prosecution had named Moulavi as the main organiser of the attacks, and had submitted what they said was a voluntary confession to the court where he had admitted his role. The court accepted the confession. However, Moulavi later told the three-judge bench hearing the case that he was not shown what he was signing and rejected the allegations against him. More than 2,300 people gave evidence for the prosecution. There were also 2,076 pieces of evidence, including explosives, swords and firearms. In the wake of the attacks, Sri Lankan authorities pointed to a "major intelligence lapse". Its parliament heard that a tip-off from India about the attacks was not properly shared with the authorities. In 2023, the Supreme Court ordered former president Maithripala Sirisena to pay millions in compensation to the victims of the bombings, after finding him responsible for national security failures that led to the attacks. Last month, two former senior officials were sentenced to death for criminal negligence that led to the bombings. Death sentences are usually commuted to life in prison in Sri Lanka due to a decades-old moratorium on executions. For years, Sri Lankans have held regular demonstrations demanding justice for the victims of the Easter attacks. The verdict on Tuesday comes as a separate investigation on former intelligence chief Suresh Sallay is under way. Sallay is accused of orchestrating the bombings with Islamist extremists. The allegations echo those aired in a 2023 documentary by British broadcaster Channel 4, which heard whistleblower testimony claiming the attacks were allowed to happen to boost the popularity of the Rajapaksa family, which long dominated Sri Lankan politics. Sallay, who was arrested in February, denies the allegations. Former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, who was elected months after the 2019 attacks, with a campaign of tackling Islamist extremism has also denied the allegations. Rajapaksa, who has been banned from leaving the country, has asked the court to prevent his potential arrest in connection with the ongoing investigations. - Published21 April 2025 - Published14 January 2022

item.title: Outrage in India over viral video of teen molested and her friend beaten
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cmz6z2vx65jeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Outrage in India over viral video of teen molested and her friend beaten - Published A video showing a teenaged girl being sexually assaulted and her male friend beaten by a group of men in India's Bihar state has sparked widespread outrage. The school students, both minors, were stopped in Jamui district on 19 September. Footage shared widely online shows them surrounded and repeatedly pleading to be allowed to leave. The boy is seen being slapped and pulled by his collar, while the girl is touched inappropriately and, in another clip, carried away by a man as the boy tries to intervene. Three accused, also minors, have been arrested in connection with the assault. A special investigation team has been set up to catch the other suspects. The disturbing footage has prompted anger over the harassment of the two teenagers and renewed a wider debate about the safety of women and girls in Bihar, as well as questions over the response of state authorities. The outrage intensified after Bihar minister Shravan Kumar said that "sporadic incidents keep happening" and that the government was keeping a watch on them. "The world is not entirely free of crime," he said, adding that those responsible would not be allowed to escape and would face strict action. Umesh Kushwaha, of the governing Janata Dal (United), also faced criticism after referring to such cases as "isolated incidents" and contrasting the government's record with that of the previous RJD administration. Kushwaha later said his remarks had been "distorted and misrepresented" and promised action against those responsible. Police said the incident took place around 19:00 local time [13:30 GMT] on Saturday, but it came to light on Monday after the video of the assault went viral. The teenagers, both students of 10th standard, attended the same coaching institute and had gone to the area to take photographs after their classes, according to police. Jamui police chief Bishwajeet Dayal said neither of them had initially reported the incident - officers began investigating after the video circulated widely online and traced the pair using the registration number of a vehicle visible in the footage. Their statements were subsequently recorded and a case was registered following a written complaint from the girl. A case has been registered under India's stringent Protection of Children from Sexual Offences Act, or Pocso. Police have also invoked sections of India's criminal code covering assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty, assault or criminal force with intent to disrobe, and acts carried out with a common intention. Senior police officer KS Anupam said three minors had been arrested and that investigators had established the involvement of two other people. Police have also begun action against 32 social media accounts accused of circulating footage in which the teenagers could be identified, she added. The shocking nature of the assault has provoked outrage online, with many social media users expressing horror and questioning why a group of men believed they had the right to confront two teenagers for being together. Some characterised the incident as an extreme form of "moral policing", while others tagged Bihar police and demanded strict action against the harassers. Shreyasi Singh, a Bihar minister and legislator from Jamui, told NDTV news channel, external the incident had brought "shame to society". Singh, a former international-level sport shooter, said women in Bihar were advancing in many areas but concerns about their safety persisted. She called for the remaining suspects to be arrested quickly and for strict action against those responsible. Opposition leaders, meanwhile, have seized on the case to question the state government's record on women's safety. Rahul Gandhi, MP and senior leader of India's main opposition Congress party, described the footage as "deeply disturbing" and said the incident reflected a patriarchal "belief that men could police a girl's body, movements and choices". "This is not culture. It is patriarchy," Gandhi wrote on X (formerly Twitter). Tejashwi Yadav, the opposition leader in Bihar, said the incident had left him "deeply ashamed" and accused the government of failing to ensure the safety of women and girls in the state. Members of Bihar's governing coalition have rejected the opposition's wider criticism of the state's law-and-order record and said those responsible for the attack would face strict action. India's National Commission for Women has also intervened, calling for all those involved to be identified and arrested and for an impartial investigation. The commission has asked for a report from Bihar police and urged authorities to prevent further sharing of the video clips to protect the girl's identity and privacy. The Bihar State Women's Commission has also sought information from district authorities about the action being taken in the case.

item.title: Four dead after powerful Typhoon Dujuan lashes Japan
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm3wj2lexl97o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Four dead after powerful Typhoon Dujuan lashes Japan - Published Four people have died in Japan after Typhoon Dujuan battered Tokyo and surrounding prefectures with torrential rains and destructive winds, local reports said. The storm cut power for 50,000 people and caused the suspension of hundreds of flights. Most evacuation orders were lifted on Tueday as the storm pulled away from Japan's eastern coast. At the height of the storm on Monday, authorities warned of an "imminent threat to life" and urged 1.9 million people to move to shelters. The fatalities were from landslides in Kanagawa and Chiba prefectures. Six others were reported missing, public broadcaster NHK reported. Dujuan had sustained winds of 130km/h (81mph) and gusts of 194km/h. The typhoon is the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", which has warmed the ocean, fuelling the formation of storms. Authorities had advised the public to pay attention to weather information. Dujuan, which is Japan's 25th typhoon of the year, hit in the midst of a five-day holiday and forced the cancellation of several events. Concerts scheduled for Monday at the Rock in Japan music festival were cancelled, while the Tokyo Game Show, a video game convention, also cancelled Monday's programme. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi offered her condolences in a post on X to those who lost their lives in the typhoon, before saying she would be continuing with her scheduled trip the United States as planned. "With a sense of urgency, I instructed Chief Cabinet Secretary Takehara and Minister Hosono to respond with utmost preparedness," she wrote, before saying she had boarded a flight to the US. She will be speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday, and will meet with US President Donald Trump. The Yokosuka City Fire Department told the BBC that a woman in Kanagawa prefecture, aged in her 60s, was believed to have been buried alive after a landslide swept the house she lived in. Following a search by rescue crews, she was found inside the home and pronounced dead, NHK reported. Separately, Sodegaura City Fire Department in Chiba prefecture told the BBC a man in his 50s was rescued after getting trapped while working to clear debris at a landslide site. The department said the worker fell into a bamboo thicket, along with some heavy machinery. He was then taken to hospital before his death was confirmed, according to local reports. Police are investigating the details of the incident. Some research suggests that Japan has become more exposed to destructive storms, but climate change is not thought to be increasing the number of these storms globally, and could even make them less common in some regions. As temperatures rise, typhoons that do form are likely to become more intense on average, however. Warmer ocean waters mean storms can pick up more energy, leading to higher wind speeds. And because a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, these storms could also bring heavier rainfall. This year, El Niño - the natural weather phenomenon bringing warmer water to parts of the tropical Pacific - is another factor. El Niño doesn't have a clear effect on the total number of typhoons, but it can affect where typhoons form, their strength and which countries they hit. Some El Niño events may expose Japan to stronger typhoons, for example. The typhoon is continuing to travel along the country's Pacific coast, heading north. The extent of the damage today may not be known until Tuesday. Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi and Mark Poynting, climate reporter - Published11 June

item.title: British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx8d38djqm25o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
British man missing after diving into Lake Como to rescue teenager - Published Italian authorities are searching for a British man who has gone missing after reportedly diving into Lake Como to rescue a teenager. The man was attempting to rescue two people - a father and son - who were in distress in the water near the San Siro municipality on the lake's western shore on Monday afternoon, Italian media report. The man and the family he was friends with had reportedly been on a boating trip at the time. The father and son were later rescued by another passing boat, but the man has not been seen again. The UK Foreign Office said: "We are supporting the family of a British national missing in Italy and are in contact with the local authorities." Emergency services - including a helicopter, divers and boat units - have responded at the scene, where the lake's depth can reach more than 200m, according to Italian news agency Ansa. Rescuers are now preparing to deploy two underwater robots to scan the lake bed where the lake becomes too deep for divers, local news site Qui Como reports. The alarm was first raised around 13:30 local time (11:30 GMT) by the mother of the teenager, who was on a rented boat around 600m from shore with her other child, it said. The man - who dived in after the father and son after they experienced difficulty swimming and was described as being in his late 30s - began to sink and was not seen resurfacing, the local newspaper reports. The mother then called emergency services. The father and son were given medical treatment after suffering from the early stages of hypothermia, according to Qui Como. Lake Como, around 30 miles north of Milan, is a popular tourist hotspot, with more than 78,000 foreign visitors in 2024, local chamber of commerce research shows. However, water temperatures there can start to fall from September onward.

item.title: Texas ICE shooting leaves Venezuelan DoorDash driver with bullet in his back, says lawyer
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3y0z25v0zjwo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Texas ICE shooting leaves Venezuelan DoorDash driver with bullet in his back, says lawyer - Published A Venezuelan DoorDash delivery driver who was shot by ICE agents was transferred from hospital to a detention centre with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer has told US media. The shooting of Wilber Rafael Garcés Perez, 28, triggered protests in Austin, Texas, on Sunday. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) said in a statement to the BBC it was investigating the shooting of a man in the Texan capital who had entered the country illegally. It was unclear what led to the shooting with the local mayor and police demanding an investigation. It comes months after a man in Houston was shot dead by an ICE officer. Attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told CBS that Garcés Perez called his wife while "yelling in pain" in hospital. She told National Public Radio he was in ICE custody. The Trump administration has ramped up immigration enforcement efforts and arrests during Trump's second term, sparking unrest across several US cities. The administration has defended its policies and the agency's controversial tactics as necessary for public safety and to enact Trump's campaign promise to secure the border and carry out mass deportations. The shooting in Austin on Sunday occurred just before 1300 local time, although details remain scarce. Dozens of protesters, some waving the flags of Mexico and Guatemala, gathered at the scene carrying signs demanding that ICE leave Austin. Local television outlets showed the demonstrators gathering across the street from a blue Toyota Corolla that sustained damage to the passenger-side door, as ICE agents stood nearby, Reuters news agency reported. Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said that Austinites have a right to know what happened and "a right to feel safe in their city" during a media briefing on Sunday. "They should know the truth," he said, adding that he is pleased that the city will also be involved in the investigation. He added that ICE operations have surged in Austin in recent weeks. ICE has faced intense scrutiny after a number of deadly shootings, including the death of Houston resident Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Salgado Araujo had not been a target of an ICE investigation, but was shot during an ICE traffic stop, according to DHS. Texas Congressman Greg Casar, a Democrat, has demanded a full and immediate independent investigation into the latest shooting and the release of body camera footage. He also demanded "accountability for any ICE officer who broke the law". Activists say that the administration has violated due process as it carries out the crackdown. Democrats have demanded reforms at the agency, including requiring immigration enforcement agents to wear body cameras and not conceal their faces. Earlier this month the US Department of Justice charged an ICE agent with lying about the non-fatal shooting of a Venezuelan migrant in Minnesota - a rare instance in which the current justice department accused a federal agent of breaking the law on the job. Earlier this week, Florida lawmaker Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican who has spoken out against the immigration crackdown, released an advert criticising the targeting and detaining of individuals who have no criminal record. Salazar appeared on the CBS programme Face the Nation on Sunday and said that she has since spoken to the president, and believes he will keep the country on the right track. "He gets it more than anybody," she said. Related topics - Published4 February - Published4 September

item.title: Canadian province sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge school shooting
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c3wyz2rkgrx0o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Canadian province sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge school shooting - Published A Canadian province is suing OpenAI over its alleged failure to notify authorities about concerning user interactions on ChatGPT prior to the Tumbler Ridge mass shooting. The company has previously apologised for not flagging Jessie Van Rootselaar's account to law enforcement before the 18-year-old killed eight people, including six children, in February. British Columbia attorney general Niki Sharma said the lawsuit, filed to a US federal court on Monday, raised questions about "the responsibilities of technology companies when they become aware of credible threats of serious violence". Families of those killed or injured in the shooting have filed separate lawsuits against OpenAI. Media reports revealed that Van Rootselaar's ChatGPT activity was flagged by OpenAI's safety team for references to gun violence months before the attack, but the company did not alert local authorities. In April, OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman apologised to the families of the victims. "I am deeply sorry that we did not alert law enforcement," Altman wrote in an open letter. The BBC has requested comment from OpenAI regarding the latest lawsuit. "To date, OpenAI has not taken meaningful steps to address the concerns raised by survivors, families and the Tumbler Ridge community," Sharma said in a statement. "The company still has an opportunity to demonstrate accountability by strengthening safeguards, improving transparency and taking concrete action to help prevent similar tragedies in the future." Speaking to reporters on Monday, Sharma said she had not read the contents of the OpenAI chats. "We have asked OpenAI to disclose these chats. They have refused. We should all be asking them: Why?" she said, according to CBC, external. Sharma said the lawsuit was filed in California, as the alleged decision not to report the shooter's ChatGPT account occurred in that US state, according to AFP. Sharma told reporters that any financial damages won by the province would go towards rebuilding the secondary school.

item.title: Infantino says he is open to talks over Fifa reform
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c639m2yggm1ro?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Infantino says he is open to talks over Fifa reform - Published Fifa president Gianni Infantino has proposed an external review of how world football's governing body operates, and says he is open to reform. In a letter sent to members of the Fifa Council and all of its national associations, Infantino explains the independent process would "recommend potential improvements". Before a meeting of the Council next month, Infantino says he is also suggesting a consultation on "how Fifa's decision-making can be further strengthened". This would include proposals on the role of the president, as well as "practical ways to strengthen transparency, participation and accountability in major strategic initiatives". Infantino has come under increasing pressure over his aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal. That would have involved selling stakes in the World Cup and other competitions to private investors, and it sparked a major backlash. In what appears to be a conciliatory gesture, Infantino writes: "Over recent weeks, I have taken time to listen before writing to you", and says the consultation will be with confederations, member associations and "relevant stakeholders". He insists that the FFE plan "did not involve relinquishing Fifa's control or authority over sporting decisions. Obviously!" His letter adds: "The proposal entered the public domain before Fifa's planned institutional process had been completed and before it could be presented in full to the Council and the member associations. I recognise that, without the full context, this caused concern and created the impression that decisions had already been taken. They had not." Infantino also claims that "democratic processes, independence and sporting authority were never for sale. They are not for sale and never will be." He states he remains "fully committed to leading Fifa and confident in what we can achieve together". Infantino's letter comes after Uefa and Concacaf - the confederations for Europe and North America, Central America and the Caribbean - demanded Fifa pays $10m to all 211 members from its cash reserves. FFE would have meant a new company being created to manage commercial and ticketing rights of all Fifa competitions, including World Cups, with 21% sold off to a private investment company. Infantino claims that the collapse of FFE "does not diminish our ambition or our responsibility to invest more of Fifa's success back into football. "We will continue to explore sustainable ways to grow Fifa's resources and expand development and solidarity support for every member association," he adds in the letter. "What changes is not the ambition, but the strength of the process through which major ideas are developed, tested and decided. "The progress we have made over the past decade gives us a strong foundation for the future. It also gives us the confidence to examine whether our governance remains suited to the scale and complexity of the decisions ahead." Earlier this month, Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt, a Fifa vice-president, told Infantino to release all documents relating to his controversial plan, and called for an independent review of FFE. Infantino will stand for election for a fourth time in March 2027, with his opponents having until 18 November to find an alternative candidate. Last month, European football's governing body Uefa began preparing criminal legal proceedings against Infantino at courts in the US over the FFE plan, demanding the release of all documents. Fifa hit back and accused Uefa of a "smear campaign against it and its leadership" in a challenge to the litigation. Infantino's tone shift represents change in bid to survive - analysis Having defiantly clung to power for weeks amid an unprecedented rebellion over his presidency, this is a significant change in tone from Infantino - and the first sign that he may feel he has no choice but to compromise if he is to win another re-election in March. On 15 October, the Fifa Council will meet for the first time since this crisis began, and Infantino will no doubt hope that this relieves some of the pressure he is under. But even if he is prepared to accept some changes to the way Fifa is run, will that be enough to win over some of those that have turned against him? Much may depend on the precise terms of reference for the external review that Infantino has proposed. After all, Infantino has not yet agreed to a similar review into his FFE plan. As well as wanting him to step down, many of Infantino's critics want an overhaul of Fifa's governance, with curbs on the president's power (such as a maximum of a single term in office), more separation between the president and the Fifa administration, greater emphasis on human rights and sustainability, and the redistribution of Fifa's cash reserves. It will be fascinating to see if Infantino is prepared to accept such changes if it means staying in power. Related topics - Published10 August - Published5 August - Published28 August

item.title: To Kill A Mockingbird first edition found in London charity shop

========================================
Harper Lee first edition novel found in Oxfam shop - Published A rare first edition of the novel To Kill A Mockingbird has been found among items donated to Oxfam, according to the charity. The copy of Harper Lee's seminal 1960 work was discovered in a box of American books given to the charity's bookshop in Portobello Road, west London. It has since been acquired by the British Library and will join its national collection. Shop manager Olivia Haysman-Walker, who identified the copy as being a first US edition, said the book could easily have been missed. "There were lots of books to work through in the donation, but we recognised To Kill A Mockingbird and thought it was worth taking a closer look." She added: "We realised quite quickly that we had something really special. "The dust jacket showed its age, and although it was worn around the edges, the pages inside were in beautiful condition. "It's amazing to think that this book has passed through our Oxfam bookshop and into the national collection at the British Library. "It really has been quite a journey, and it's a lovely reminder, during Second Hand September, of the kind of treasures that can be hiding among the shelves and donations in our shops." Second Hand September is Oxfam's annual campaign encouraging people to buy second-hand. Lee's Pulitzer Prize-winning book tells the story of lawyer Atticus Finch as he defends Tom Robinson, a black man wrongly accused of raping a white woman. Her story of racial injustice and childhood innocence, set in Alabama in 1934, has sold more than 40 million copies around the world and has been translated into 40 languages. The US novelist, who was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, died in 2016 at the age of 89. item.title: First UK charges brought over 1994 Rwanda genocide
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cr2092216nywo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
First UK charges brought over 1994 Rwanda genocide - Published A Rwandan man, who has been living in north London, has become the first person charged in the UK with offences relating to the 1994 Rwanda genocide, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has said. Dr Vincent Brown, formerly Dr Vincent Bajinya, 65, has been charged with one offence of conduct ancillary to genocide and six offences of conduct ancillary to murder as a crime against humanity. Frank Ferguson, head of the CPS's Special Crime and Counter Terrorism Division, said Brown "is alleged to have directed and incited acts of murder and genocide carried out by others". Brown will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday. Ferguson said the decision to charge Brown was made "after reviewing a file of evidence submitted by the War Crimes Team at the Metropolitan Police". "We concluded that our legal test for bringing criminal charges had been met," he added. The War Crimes Team began their investigation in September 2019 after a formal request from the Rwandan government to investigate people allegedly involved in a genocide in the Rugenge district of Kigali in April 1994. Over the course of 100 days in 1994, an estimated 800,000 ethnic Tutsis and politically moderate Hutus people were killed in Rwanda by Hutu extremists. They were targeting members of the minority Tutsi community, as well as their political opponents, irrespective of their ethnic origin. The mainly Tutsi forces who took power following the genocide were alleged to have killed thousands of Hutu people in Rwanda in retaliation. The Metropolitan Police said the charges against Brown follow "a complex and extensive seven-year investigation". Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "This case demonstrates the UK is not a safe haven for individuals suspected of committing international crimes. "The War Crimes Teams remains committed to ensuring those suspected of involvement in genocide and other atrocity crimes are held accountable through due legal process. "A number of other investigations remain ongoing into other individuals in the UK for similar offences related to the genocide in Rwanda."

item.title: Merz vows to keep coalition together for Germany's 'democratic future'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqm27p8enwmko?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Merz vows to keep coalition together for Germany's 'democratic future' - Published German Chancellor Friedrich Merz says he will keep his ruling coalition together for the sake of his country's "democratic future", following resounding defeats for his party in two state elections. "We are determined to live up to the historic challenges our country is facing," Merz said, referring to the coalition between his Christian Democratic Unionist (CDU) party and the Social Democratic Party (SPD). Merz's position has come under mounting pressure after Sunday's election results. In the north-eastern Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party won the most votes, with the CDU failing even to reach the threshold to stay in the state parliament. Meanwhile in Berlin, the CDU came second to the hard-left Die Linke party, with the AfD also making significant gains. - Katya Adler: Merz's political crisis threatens Germany's obsession with stability - Published21 hours ago Speaking at the news conference on Monday, Merz described the result in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern as "a heavy blow" for the centre-right CDU. "This election is a profound turning point. It is a dramatic, unprecedented result for the CDU in Germany," he acknowledged. Merz said there had been no discussion about his own position since the results and pushed back against the idea that his low popularity ratings alone were behind the election defeats. "I know that I as an individual played a role in these state elections," Merz said, before adding: "But the reasons for the results go far beyond just me." "We are witnessing a profound transformation of Germany's political party system, as is happening in many other countries around the world." There have been rumours Merz, who has only been in power for 16 months, could be replaced mid-term in a so-called chancellor swap due to his poor approval ratings. Asked earlier on Monday how long Merz has left in office, the AfD's co-leader Alice Weidel told the BBC: "Pretty soon, he's going to leave." The two elections took place on Sunday, a fortnight after the CDU saw its vote halved in the state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD won a major victory. In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, the CDU fell short of a 5% threshold to enter parliament, underperforming against what had already been projected to be the party's worst ever result in the area. Merz earlier conceded that this result was "a disaster". While the AfD won the most votes in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, it was far short of a majority and is unlikely to govern as other parties may refuse to work with it. Some branches of the party are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation it strongly rejects. But its anti-immigration, Germany first, and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east. In Berlin, the CDU's defeat means Die Linke, which won the most votes, could now take power in a coalition. Elif Eralp, who led the party to victory in the capital, promised to tackle unaffordable rent prices in remarks made after the results came out. "The people of Berlin have clearly opted for a change in policy, specifically for an affordable Berlin, for policies that solve the rent crisis and put people first," she told German news outlet The Pioneer. During the election campaign, Eralp pledged to expropriate more than 200,000 housing units from private landlords. Merz has promised to pursue legislation to prevent such actions, citing the impact on foreign investment.

item.title: Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx4gqv239043o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Russia's elections had few surprises - but how the Kremlin uses the results will be crucial - Published Many things about Russia are hard to predict. The result of this election wasn't one of them. In a political system tightly controlled by the Kremlin, the party of power – United Russia –had been widely expected to remain the largest in parliament by a large margin. There were no upsets. No surprises. No other party came close. Preliminary results suggest that United Russia, which is supported by President Putin, is on course to retain its constitutional majority in the State Duma - with even bigger numbers than last time round. And that's after more than four-and-half years of war on Ukraine, which have resulted in massive battlefield losses for the Russian army, economic difficulties and, most recently, widespread petrol shortages due to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil facilities. Those parties trailing far behind, but which have cleared the 5% threshold and made it into the new Duma, featured in the previous parliament, too: a Duma that was fully behind the Kremlin and the so-called special military operation. One party that didn't make it into parliament was Yabloko. Yabloko had been the only anti-war political party permitted to take part in the election - permission that was short-lived. Just twelve days after being registered for the vote it was removed from the ballot (the party list) by the Supreme Court, an indication of Kremlin concern that Yabloko's pro-peace message was gaining too much traction with the public. The party isn't surprised that the new Duma looks like being as pro-Kremlin as the previous one. "What other result can there be if there were ten parties on the ballot and they all support the policies of Putin?" Yabloko party chairman Nikolai Rybakov tells me. "I don't think the Duma will change. They'll vote 100% for the policies of Putin just like they did." Although Yabloko had been struck off the party list, around a hundred of its candidates remained in individual constituency races. According to preliminary results, none have won seats. The party claims it has come under sustained pressure. "Some of our candidates, who should have been running, are in jail, many were barred from running and some of our election observers weren't registered and were unable to keep an eye on the voting," Nikolai says. Ahead of the final day of this three-day election, Ukraine launched a large-scale drone attack on the Moscow area. Three people were killed in Moscow Region, while in the capital the city's oil refinery was hit. At a polling station near the oil refinery, I spoke to voters about the attack. There was no sense of surprise. More a quiet resignation. With Russia's war on Ukraine now in its fifth year, Muscovites have grown used to their city periodically becoming a front line. "People in the Donbas, as well as in Bryansk, and Belgorod near the Ukrainian border, hear this kind of thing every day," a voter called Viktor told me. "And they just get on with their lives." The outcome of this election was predictable. What happens next is less clear. The Kremlin is likely to use the result to claim that most Russians have rallied behind the president, and to justify future policies and subsequent decisions on the course of the war. The key question: what will those decisions be? President Putin recently ruled out another wave of mobilisation. "There is no scenario today that would require it," he declared. Not today, then. But what about tomorrow? Despite official denials, in Russian society there remains deep anxiety about the possibility of a new round of mobilisation. At the very least, the Kremlin is likely to treat the election result as a 'mandate from the people' to continue the war. Related topics - Published3 days ago - Published3 days ago

item.title: Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance
item.description:

========================================
Seven Ethiopian rebel groups form new alliance - Published Several of the rebel groups which have been fighting the Ethiopian authorities in different parts of the country have announced they have formed an alliance to remove the government in Addis Ababa. The alliance brings together the Fano militia in Amhara, the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and four other smaller groupings in a coalition named Alliance for Survival. The seven groups accuse Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of presiding over "war, genocide, mass destruction and utter poverty", claiming Ethiopia is at risk of disintegration. Abiy's spokesperson Billene Seyoum said the groups had already been collaborating for some time, Reuters reports. The BBC has asked the government for comment. Ethiopia has faced years of armed conflict in Oromia and Amhara, the most populous states in the country. There have also been renewed tensions in the northern Tigray region, where a two-year civil war left hundreds of thousands dead and displaced millions. An African-Union peace deal ended that war in 2022, but there have been fears of a return to a full-scale conflict, with both sides accusing each other of violating that agreement. Besides Oromia, Amhara and Tigray, the new alliance also includes groups based in three other regions - Somali, Afar and Benishangul-Gumuz – making up a half of Ethiopia's 12 regional states. The states are structured largely based on their dominant ethnic groups – a system of ethnic federalism that gives some autonomy to the states, but which can present social and political challenges for the country which has more than 80 ethnic groups. Some of the rebel groups in the new alliance have previously fought against each other but they say they will now work together against their common enemy. However, analyst Edward Bach from advisory firm Verisk Maplecroft told the AFP news agency that the groups were "unlikely to share weapons... as your ally today can be your enemy tomorrow". Amhara's Fano group fought alongside federal forces against the TPLF during the Tigray war. It however turned against the federal government in an armed insurgency less than a year after the war ended, after refusing government orders to disarm. Abdikadir Addaani Hirmooge, the spokesman for the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), which is part of the alliance, told the BBC that the groups in the new coalition were working to bring together communities that have been divided against one another. "Our objective is for the communities to have democracy and to exercise their right to self-determination, to genuinely govern themselves," he said. He said that the government had not respected a peace deal signed in 2018 to end the conflict in the Somali region. "Ethnic conflict, insecurity, and mutual oppression and pushing each other aside have not been eradicated, resulting in a need that has affected every ethnic group," he said. The government has been fighting the OLA since 2018. The announcement of the Alliance for Survival coalition comes months after reports of an alleged alliance between TPLF and neighbouring Eritrea. Abiy responded by saying he had faith in Ethiopia's "defensive capabilities". "Even if others were added, we do not have an iota of fear regarding Ethiopia's sovereignty," he told lawmakers in July. The country held a general election in June, with Abiy's Prosperity Party retaining its overwhelming parliamentary majority, despite the poll being overshadowed by conflict, accusations of repression and little participation by opposition parties. The Fano and OLA rebel groups rejected the election and its results. The Tigray region and its six million inhabitants were completely excluded from the poll. item.title: US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5ye7v88qy7o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
US strikes on alleged drug boats could be crimes against humanity, says UN - Published A UN report has concluded that recent US airstrikes on vessels allegedly trafficking drugs breached international law and could constitute crimes against humanity. The report by Special Rapporteur Ben Saul said since September last year there had been at least 68 US strikes in the Caribbean and Pacific, outside US territorial waters, which killed more than 220 people. Saul said that even if targets could be identified as members of designated terrorist groups, they had not staged an armed attack on the US which would trigger a right to self-defence under international law. The report comes two days after the US military said it killed four people in a strike on a vessel in the Caribbean. "Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking. The operation killed four narco-terrorists," Southcom, which commands US forces in the region, said in a statement about the latest attack, which was accompanied by a grainy video. But in a briefing note released by the UN Human Rights Council on Monday, Saul said that "such attacks amount to serial extrajudicial killings in violation of the right to life, being unjustified in national or personal self-defence or under international humanitarian law, the international law of the sea, narcotics suppression conventions, or international counter-terrorism law". "There are reasonable grounds to believe that the reported 68 attacks that killed 223 people constituted crimes against humanity of murder under customary international law," Saul concluded. BBC News has contacted the White House and State Department for a response to the report. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has previously said the overall operation is aimed at removing "narco-terrorists from our hemisphere" and securing the US from "the drugs that are killing our people". The US military launched the operation, known as "Southern Spear", in early September. However, officials have not offered definitive evidence that the vessels targeted are involved in trafficking. Since the beginning, experts have questioned the legality of the strikes, which initially drew strong criticism from Latin American leaders whose citizens have been targeted. However, Nicolás Maduro, who was the Venezuelan leader at the time and opposed the strikes, was seized by US forces in a dramatic and highly controversial night-time raid on the capital Caracas at the beginning of this year. Another outspoken critic of Operation Southern Spear, Colombia's left-wing president at the time, Gustavo Petro, stood down in August after a Trump-backed candidate won June's presidential election. Two charged with woman's murder as South Africa police investigate eight other body finds - Published Two women have been charged in South Africa in connection with the murder of a woman in an area east of Johannesburg – the last of nine recent cases in that region that have reignited the debate about the levels of gender-based violence in the country. Under pressure to solve the spate of murders which has involved victims' bodies being dumped on a roadside, police have described the arrests of the two as a "breakthrough". Referring to all nine cases, acting police chief Lt Gen Puleng Dimpane said her officers were "working tirelessly to bring those responsible to justice". The two women have been charged with premeditated murder and defeating the ends of justice. A man who was also arrested has been released without charge. Their case relates to the death of Jabulile Ntimba, whose half-naked body was found wrapped in a sheet in Dawn Park last Thursday. Several of the recent victims were discovered partially clothed and with injuries, but police have stressed that they have not established whether all the deaths are connected or whether a serial killer is responsible. Addressing journalists on Monday, deputy police chief Lt Gen Tebello Mosikili said that "a team of analysts are working hard to see if there are links to all these cases" but the killing of Ntimba "appears to be an indication of a murder that stemmed from a relationship... this includes... a possible love triangle". South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence in the world. It also has a very high murder rate and though officials statistics do not identify the gender of the victims, a recent estimate from the country's Human Rights Commission indicated that, on average, six women were murdered every day between April and June this year. The recent grim discoveries have sparked a national outcry about the scale of the problem and increased the feeling of insecurity for many women.
